title: Production and Detection of Polarized Light
short_intro: Polarized light refers to transverse electromagnetic waves in which electric field oscillations are restricted to a single plane. The production and detection of polarized light rely on fundamental wave phenomena such as reflection, refraction, double refraction, selective absorption, and scattering.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definitions of polarization, Brewster's law, Malus's law, Polaroid sheets, and polarization by reflection and refraction.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Double refraction in uniaxial crystals, positive and negative crystals, Huygens' explanation of ordinary and extraordinary rays, Nicol prism, quarter-wave and half-wave plates, and analysis of elliptically and circularly polarized light.

prerequisites: Snell's law of refraction and total internal reflection

concept_notes.heading: Polarization by Reflection and Brewster's Law
bullets: When unpolarized light is incident on a transparent dielectric surface at a specific angle called the polarizing angle (or Brewster's angle, i_p), the reflected light is completely plane-polarized with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected ray and the refracted ray are mutually perpendicular to each other.
Brewster's law is expressed mathematically as tan(i_p) = n, where n is the refractive index of the medium.

concept_notes.heading: Selective Absorption and Polaroids
bullets: Certain naturally occurring and synthetic crystalline materials possess dichroism, which is the property of selectively absorbing one of the mutually perpendicular components of polarized light while transmitting the other.
Polaroids are manufactured sheets containing microscopic crystals of quinine iodosulfate oriented parallel to one another in a plastic matrix.
When polarized light passes through a polarizer (analyzer), the transmitted intensity varies according to Malus's law: I = I_0 cos²(θ).

concept_notes.heading: Double Refraction (Birefringence)
bullets: When an unpolarized light ray enters an anisotropic crystal such as calcite (CaCO_3) or quartz, it splits into two refracted rays known as the Ordinary ray (O-ray) and the Extraordinary ray (E-ray).
The O-ray obeys ordinary laws of refraction and travels with the same speed in all directions within the crystal, whereas the E-ray does not obey Snell's law and its speed varies with direction.
In negative crystals like calcite, the velocity of the E-ray is greater than that of the O-ray (v_e > v_o), whereas in positive crystals like quartz, v_o > v_e.

concept_notes.heading: Production and Detection of Elliptically and Circularly Polarized Light
bullets: Circularly polarized light is produced when two mutually perpendicular plane-polarized beams of equal amplitude, having a phase difference of odd multiples of π/2, are superimposed.
Elliptically polarized light results from the superposition of two mutually perpendicular plane-polarized beams of unequal amplitudes with a phase difference of (π/2 ± mπ).

Detection involves passing the beam through a quarter-wave plate followed by an analyzer; circular light shows constant intensity while rotated, whereas unpolarized light shows no intensity variation.

derivations.title: Brewster's Law Derivation
derivations.conditions: Light incident on a dielectric boundary at polarizing angle i_p
steps: Let unpolarized light be incident at angle i_p such that the reflected ray is completely polarized.
According to Snell's law at the interface, sin(i_p) / sin(r) = n_2 / n_1 = n, where r is the angle of refraction.
At the polarizing angle, the reflected ray and refracted ray are perpendicular, so i_p + r = 90°, which gives r = 90° - i_p.
Substitute r into Snell's law: sin(i_p) / sin(90° - i_p) = n.
Since sin(90° - i_p) = cos(i_p), sin(i_p) / cos(i_p) = tan(i_p) = n.

derivations.title: Malus's Law Derivation
derivations.conditions: Plane-polarized light of intensity I_0 incident on an analyzer with transmission axis at angle θ
s: Let the amplitude of the electric field vector of the incident plane-polarized light be E_0.

When this light passes through an analyzer whose transmission axis makes an angle θ with the vibration direction of the incident light, the electric field vector resolves into two components: E_0 cos(θ) parallel to the axis and E_0 sin(θ) perpendicular to the axis.
The analyzer transmits only the component parallel to its transmission axis, E = E_0 cos(θ).
Since the intensity of light is proportional to the square of the amplitude of the electric field (I ∝ E²), the transmitted intensity I is proportional to (E_0 cos(θ))².
Therefore, I = I_0 cos²(θ) where I_0 is the maximum intensity transmitted when θ = 0.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity Variation of Polarized Light (Malus's Law Verification)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A polar plot or Cartesian plot of transmitted intensity I versus angle θ showing a periodic curve proportional to cos²(θ), with maxima at 0°, 180°, 360° and zeroes at 90°, 270°.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that light is a transverse wave, as longitudinal waves would show no variation in intensity upon rotation of the analyzer.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems calculating intensity ratios at specific angles like 30°, 45°, 60°.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nicol Prism Construction and Action
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rhombic calcite crystal cut along the diagonal, cemented with Canada balsam, showing total internal reflection of the ordinary ray and transmission of the extraordinary ray.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Canada balsam has a refractive index (1.55) intermediate between the O-ray (1.658) and E-ray (1.486) of calcite for sodium light, allowing the O-ray to undergo total internal reflection while the E-ray passes through.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions regarding the function of Canada balsam and the elimination of the ordinary ray.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Polarization by Reflection Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A ray of unpolarized light striking a glass plate at angle i_p, splitting into a reflected ray at 90° to the refracted ray, with perpendicular electric vector symbols on the reflected ray.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visually validates Brewster's condition where reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Drawing ray diagrams and calculating refractive index given the polarizing angle.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the polarizing angle for a glass surface of refractive index 1.732. (Given tan(60°) = 1.732)
solution_steps: Substitute the given value of refractive index: tan(i_p) = 1.732.
Find the angle whose tangent is 1.732: i_p = 60°.

solved_numericals.question: Unpolarized light of intensity 32 W/m² is incident on a polarizer. The transmitted light is then passed through an analyzer whose transmission axis makes an angle of 45° with the polarizer. Find the intensity of light coming out of the analyzer.
solution_steps: Intensity after passing through the first polarizer (I_0) is half of the incident unpolarized light: I_0 = 32 / 2 = 16 W/m².
Apply Malus's law for the analyzer at angle θ = 45°: I = I_0 cos²(θ).

solved_numericals.question: A quarter-wave plate is designed for sodium light of wavelength 589 nm. Calculate the minimum thickness of the calcite plate if the ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices are n_o = 1.658 and n_e = 1.486 respectively.
solution_steps: Write the formula for the thickness of a quarter-wave plate: d = λ / [4(n_o - n_e)].
Substitute the given values: λ = 589 * 10^-9 m, n_o = 1.658, n_e = 1.486.
Calculate the refractive index difference: n_o - n_e = 1.658 - 1.486 = 0.172.

assumptions_and_limitations: Brewster's law assumes non-magnetic dielectric media where relative magnetic permeability μ_r = 1.
Uniaxial crystal formulas assume monochromatic light and normal incidence parallel to specific crystal cuts.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Unpolarized light can be converted into circularly polarized light directly using a single polarizer.
common_misconceptions.correct: Circularly polarized light is produced by superimposing two mutually perpendicular plane-polarized beams with a phase difference of π/2.
common_misconceptions.why: A single polarizer only produces plane-polarized light from unpolarized light.

common_misconceptions.correct: Only transverse waves can be polarized.
common_misconceptions.why: Polarization requires oscillations to occur perpendicular to the direction of propagation, which is impossible in longitudinal waves where oscillations are parallel.

quick_revision: At Brewster's angle, reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, and tan(i_p) = n.
